source: Lee et al. (2025) Learning to Refine at Test-Time via Intrinsic Self-Verification (ReVISE)
finding: ReVISE adds [refine] and [eos] tokens. The model learns to decide after each answer whether to stop or refine. Trained by SFT then a DPO curriculum. It beats SFT, RFT and STaR+ at Maj@1 and Maj@5.
numbers: Table 1. Llama-3.2-1B GSM8K Maj@1 28.1 vs RFT 26.2, STaR+ 26.2, SFT 22.1, few-shot CoT 5.7. MATH-500 13.4 vs RFT 12.6. Llama-3.1-8B GSM8K 61.6 vs 59.2 best baseline; MATH-500 33.6 vs RFT 30.8, SFT 27.8, CoT 23.4. Maj@5 8B: GSM8K 69.2, MATH-500 37.6.
limits: Gains over the best baseline are 1 to 3 points. Table 1 is single runs with no seeds. Small Llama models only. Training uses gold GSM8K/MATH data.
agent_relevance: A trained stop-or-refine trigger helps a little. Our scaffold has no training, so the S5 trigger must come from prompts or external signals.

source: Lee et al. (2025) Learning to Refine at Test-Time via Intrinsic Self-Verification (ReVISE) - verifier quality
finding: The refine trigger is the gap between [eos] and [refine] token probability. Curriculum training raises self-verification AUROC. It also beats a separate V-STaR verifier.
numbers: Fig 3b: AUROC 71% without curriculum vs 76% with two-stage curriculum (Llama-3.2-1B, GSM8K). Table 7: V-STaR verifier 69.5 vs ReVISE 76.0. Stage 2 training slightly lowers verification accuracy.
limits: AUROC 76% is far from reliable: about a quarter of ranked pairs are wrong. 1B model only.
agent_relevance: A usable trigger is only moderately accurate even after training. Treat any S5 trigger as a noisy signal, not a trusted gate.

source: Lee et al. (2025) Learning to Refine at Test-Time via Intrinsic Self-Verification (ReVISE) - ablations
finding: Preference loss and curriculum both matter. Refinement is real, not just resampling: it beats First (stop at first answer) and Retry (resample).
numbers: Fig 4: removing DPO loss drops accuracy by 10.3 points. Fig 3a: no curriculum 22.6% vs curriculum 28.1% on GSM8K (1B). Table 5: plain DPO 22.6 GSM8K, 10.8 MATH-500 vs ReVISE 28.1, 13.4. Fig 8: 8B MATH-500 keeps improving with up to 3 refinement rounds.
limits: Ablations on the 1B model only. Iteration gains in Fig 8 are read from a plot.
agent_relevance: The decision of when to refine is learned jointly with how. Copying only the how loses much of the gain.

source: Lee et al. (2025) Learning to Refine at Test-Time via Intrinsic Self-Verification (ReVISE) - confidence-weighted voting and transfer
finding: Using the model's own [eos] confidence as the vote weight beats plain majority and likelihood weighting. Gains hold up to 64 samples. Transfer to another domain gives small gains. Code also gains a little.
numbers: Fig 6: 8 samples, M([eos]) weighting 33.9% vs unweighted 33.2% vs likelihood 32.7%. Table 8 GSM8K 1B: Maj@64 ReVISE 37.7 vs 31.6 to 33.2 for baselines. Table 4 (train MATH, test GSM8K): 8B ReVISE 61.5 vs SFT 60.3, RFT 60.3; 1B 8.8 vs 8.2. Table 2 MBPP Pass@1 33.1 vs STaR+ 30.7, SFT 30.0.
limits: Weighting gain of 0.7 points is near noise. Table 8 reports sd of 0.1 to 1.1.
agent_relevance: Confidence-weighted voting over several scaffold attempts is cheap and plausible for our selection step.

source: Lee et al. (2025) Learning to Refine at Test-Time via Intrinsic Self-Verification (ReVISE) - comparison with SCoRe
finding: On Gemma-2-2B, ReVISE matches SCoRe on MATH-500 at about 1/30 of the generation cost. More training rounds add gains.
numbers: Table 6: zero-shot CoT 16.8, SFT 17.6, RFT 18.6, SCoRe 23.0, ReVISE 23.2, +iter1 24.2, +iter2 25.8. SCoRe about 1.5M generations; ReVISE 50k.
limits: SCoRe number is copied from its paper (no open code), so this is not a controlled replication. Different base model than SCoRe's Gemini.
agent_relevance: Cheap learned triggers may match costly RL. Author-reported only.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe)
finding: Offline fine-tuning on correction traces (STaR, Pair-SFT) barely helps self-correction. Two failure modes: distribution shift, and collapse to making no edits. The base model's self-correction is negative.
numbers: Table 2, Gemini 1.5 Flash, MATH: base Acc@t1 52.6, Acc@t2 41.4 (delta -11.2). Self-Refine -1.0. STaR +0.4. Pair-SFT +1.8. Right-to-wrong rate of base 15.8%.
limits: Gemini models only. One benchmark in this table.
agent_relevance: A model not trained for revision tends to damage correct answers. S5 should block revision when no real defect is shown.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe) - result
finding: Multi-turn online RL with a progress reward gives the first clearly positive intrinsic correction gain. It works mostly by not breaking correct answers.
numbers: MATH: SCoRe Acc@t1 60.0, Acc@t2 64.4, delta +4.4; incorrect-to-correct 5.8%, correct-to-incorrect 1.4% (base 15.8%). Table 3 HumanEval: SCoRe t2 64.6 vs t1 52.4, delta +12.2; Self-Refine -1.2, Pair-SFT -1.8.
limits: Same-lab, same-family models. Heavy RL training. A delta of 4.4 on MATH is modest. No independent replication in these sources (ReVISE only copies its number).
agent_relevance: Most of the gain is a lower right-to-wrong rate. This supports a guardrail: when a check passes, keep the answer.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: With oracle labels deciding when to stop, self-correction looks great. Without oracle labels, intrinsic correction lowers accuracy. This is the baseline critique that learned triggers must beat.
numbers: Table 2 oracle: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5; GPT-4 84.3 to 97.5. Table 3 no oracle: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 74.7 (round 2), CommonsenseQA 75.8 to 41.8; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0. Table 4: GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5 to 88.0 and 90.0; Llama-2 62.0 to 36.5.
limits: Prompted self-correction only, no fine-tuning. Prompt wording and temperature were later contested (see Liu et al.).
agent_relevance: The oracle gap (up to about 20 points) is the value of a good trigger.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet - equal-compute comparison
finding: Multi-agent debate does no better than self-consistency at the same number of responses. Gains from debate may be just more samples.
numbers: Table 7 GSM8K (GPT-3.5): single response 76.7; self-consistency 3 responses 82.5, 6: 85.3, 9: 88.2; debate about 83 at 6 and 9 responses.
limits: Table layout is partly garbled in text extraction, so debate cells are approximate.
agent_relevance: Compare any refinement loop against sampling the same number of answers and voting.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey
finding: Three-part verdict: no prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs in general tasks; correction works when reliable external feedback exists; large-scale fine-tuning enables it. Many positive results use impractical setups.
numbers: Qualitative survey of many papers. Table 4 lists unfair settings (oracle stop, weak initial prompts, unequal compute).
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs
limits: Survey, not new experiments. Verdict is conditional on papers up to mid 2024. Later RL methods (ReVISE, S2R, SPOC) came after or alongside.
agent_relevance: Supports external tools for verification at S5, and trained triggers only where available.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Mistake finding is the bottleneck, not correction. Models are poor at locating the first wrong step in chain-of-thought traces, even in objective tasks.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake, five tasks. Best model GPT-4 reaches 52.87 overall mistake-location accuracy with direct step prompting. Traces sampled 15% correct, 85% incorrect (300 per task in some tasks: 255 incorrect, 45 correct). Word sorting GPT-4 62.29 and 65.33 in two prompt modes; GPT-3.5-Turbo 10.10 in one cell.
limits: Tasks are word sorting, tracking, logic deduction, arithmetic, Dyck, not natural math. Prompting only. Some model cells missing.
agent_relevance: Checks must target step-level errors. Asking the model to find its own error is unreliable.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location - backtracking with location
finding: Given the true error location, correction gains are large. With a random location, gains shrink and correct answers get broken more. A mistake-finder needs fairly high accuracy.
numbers: Table 6, PaLM 2 Unicorn: with true location, change on originally-correct traces -11.11 to 0 and on incorrect traces +18.04 to +43.92 (multistep arithmetic +43.92); with random location, correct-trace loss -6.67 to -15.91, incorrect gain +5.16 to +21.57. Fig 3: losses plateau near 65% classifier accuracy. A small trained classifier (Table 7) beats 3-shot prompting in 4 of 5 tasks but is below the needed threshold.
limits: Gold locations are human annotated. Classifier was trained out of domain.
agent_relevance: A cheap step-locator near 65% accuracy may be enough to pay off. A bad one hurts correct answers.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Small Language Models Need Strong Verifiers to Self-Correct Reasoning (SCORE)
finding: A small refiner fine-tuned on its own filtered critiques improves, but only with a strong verifier. Self-verification by the same small model adds little. Verification is the bottleneck.
numbers: Table 2, LLaMA-2-13B-chat GSM8K: self-verifier + SCORE refiner correction frequency 19.0%, contribution 10.8%; GPT-4 verifier 63.3% and 15.6%; oracle 62.8% and 14.0%. Gemma-7b-it with GPT-4 verifier: average +8.3 across five datasets. Refiner transfers to unseen data (up to +12.1 on a MATH subset); the verifier does not transfer.
limits: Two small models (13B, 7B). GPT-4 as verifier is not self-contained.
agent_relevance: The refiner skill can be had cheaply but the stop-or-refine decision cannot. Spend effort on the S5 check, using external or stronger checks.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Large Language Models Have Intrinsic Self-Correction Ability
finding: A counter-claim: intrinsic self-correction works with zero temperature and fair (non-leading) prompts. Non-zero temperature and biased prompts explain earlier failures. Effects are small.
numbers: Table 4 GPT-3.5 CommonsenseQA, unbiased prompt: temp 0 75.92 to 76.00; temp 0.5 75.51 to 74.86; temp 1.0 74.45 to 72.56 (-1.89). Table 2: biased prompt set 1 GPT-4 CSQA 84.11 to 66.34; fair set 3 84.60. GPT-3.5 HotpotQA 31.0 to 47.0 on set 3.
limits: Fair-prompt gains on CSQA are tiny (+0.08 to +0.6). HotpotQA numbers look like N=100, so noisy. Not a full refutation of Huang.
agent_relevance: Prompt wording matters: do not tell the model its answer may be wrong. Keep the verify pass deterministic.

source: Jiang et al. (2024) Self-[In]Correct: LLMs Struggle with Discriminating Self-Generated Responses
finding: Models are not reliably better at judging their prior outputs than generating them. This undercuts the premise of refine-by-judging. The gap grows with model strength but stays small.
numbers: In 54 of 56 experiments the hypothesis (discrimination is not better than generation) is not rejected, p<0.05. The strongest models (Llama-3-70B, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4-turbo) show a small positive discrimination-minus-generation gap on nearly all tasks.
limits: Discrimination measured on a fixed task set in a choice format. Instruction tuning did not help discrimination.
agent_relevance: A self-judge for the S5 trigger gets weaker as the model gets weaker. Prefer verifiers that use extra information (tools, tests, a different view).

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
finding: Self-Refine helps strongly on preference-judged tasks and gives nothing on math. The cause is that the model cannot see errors in its own reasoning.
numbers: Sentiment reversal GPT-4 3.8 to 36.2; dialogue GPT-3.5 36.4 to 63.6; math reasoning GPT-3.5 64.1 to 64.1 (0 gain). ChatGPT feedback said everything looks good on 94% of math instances. With an external error detector, math gains exceed 5%.
quote: a consistent-looking reasoning chain can deceive LLMs
limits: The headline +20% average comes from subjective tasks scored by preference. Math, the verifiable task, gets zero.
agent_relevance: Self-feedback improves style, not correctness. A learned or external trigger is needed for reasoning.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Large models are calibrated on multiple choice and can score P(True) for their own answers. Self-evaluation improves with scale and when the model sees many of its own samples first. P(IK) generalises partially; calibration is poor on new tasks.
numbers: Qualitative from abstract and introduction. Exact AUROC figures live in plots and were not extracted.
limits: Needs large models and in-distribution tasks. Calibration breaks out of distribution.
agent_relevance: Supports a probability-style confidence as the S5 trigger, shown alongside sampled alternatives.

source: Lightman et al. (2023) Let's Verify Step by Step
finding: Process supervision (step-level labels) beats outcome supervision for training reward models on MATH. Active learning helps. PRM800K released.
numbers: Process-supervised model solves 78% of a representative MATH test subset. PRM800K has 800,000 step-level human labels.
limits: Only abstract-level figures were extracted. Human labelling is costly.
agent_relevance: A step-level checker is the proven way to locate errors, which matches the need shown by Tyen et al.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Generative Verifiers: Reward Modeling as Next-Token Prediction (GenRM)
finding: A verifier that writes a chain-of-thought critique before judging beats discriminative verifiers and LLM-as-judge in Best-of-N. It also scales with test-time compute.
numbers: Abstract: Best-of-N up from 5% to 45.3% on algorithmic tasks and 73% to 93.4% on GSM8K; easy-to-hard: 28% to 44.6% on MATH, 37.9% to 53.5% on MMLU abstract algebra.
limits: Abstract-level numbers only. The verifier is a separately trained model, not the generator itself.
agent_relevance: A reasoning verifier, voted over several samples, is stronger than a one-token yes/no check.

source: Ma et al. (2025) S2R: Teaching LLMs to Self-verify and Self-correct via RL
finding: A small SFT start (3.1k self-verify and self-correct samples) plus outcome and process RL makes a 7B model verify and correct itself, with high data efficiency.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Math-7B improved from 51.0% to 81.6% (abstract). Table 2 text: +32.2% on MATH500 and +34.3% on GSM8K over the base model.
limits: Some Table 2 cells are hard to align in text extraction, so only the stated improvements are recorded. Base model is heavily math-pretrained. Authors' own baselines.
agent_relevance: Another independent trained verify-then-correct method gives large gains, but through RL that a scaffold cannot do.

source: Zhao et al. (2025) SPOC: Spontaneous Self-Correction via interleaved solution and verification
finding: A single model alternates solving and verifying and stops when verification says correct. Gains are larger on the small model. Large models are right at turn 1, so the correction delta shrinks.
numbers: Abstract: Llama-3.1-8B and 70B gain 8.8 and 11.6 on MATH500, 10.0 and 20.0 on AMC23, 3.3 and 6.7 on AIME24. Table 4 (8B): base 52.2/22.5/3.3 vs SPOC-Corr 61.0/32.5/6.7. Appendix C.1: verifier accuracy depends on solution accuracy; on easy tasks it predicts correct more often (higher TP and FP).
limits: AMC23 and AIME24 are tiny (40 and 30 problems), so a 3.3 gain is one problem. Verifiers lean toward saying correct on easy tasks.
agent_relevance: Shows the verify-then-stop pattern. Report the false-accept rate before trusting a stop signal.

source: Cross-paper synthesis: oracle gap versus learned trigger
finding: Across Huang, SCoRe, Tyen and ReVISE, a perfect trigger gives 10 to 20 points, prompted triggers give losses, and trained triggers recover about 1 to 5 points.
numbers: Oracle: GSM8K +19.6 (GPT-3.5), +13.2 (GPT-4). Prompted: -1 to -34 points (Llama-2 62.0 to 36.5). SCoRe +4.4 (MATH). ReVISE Maj@1 +1.9 to +2.8 over the best baseline (1B and 8B GSM8K).
limits: Different models, tasks, and metrics. Compared by hand, not a meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: A learned trigger captures a fraction of the oracle gap. Plan for small gains and measure the right-to-wrong rate directly.

source: Rival explanations: model cannot judge versus setup bias (Huang, Jiang, Tyen vs Liu)
finding: Two competing explanations for failed prompted self-correction: the model cannot judge its own output (Huang, Jiang, Tyen), or the setup is biased by prompt wording and temperature (Liu). Jiang and Tyen test judging directly and find it weak. Liu varies prompt and temperature and finds sign flips.
numbers: Liu: temp 1.0 gives -1.89 on CSQA, fair prompt at temp 0 gives +0.08. Jiang: 54 of 56 tests fail to show discrimination better than generation. Tyen: best mistake location 52.87.
limits: Both sides rely on small effects. The direct discrimination tests are the stronger discriminating experiments.
agent_relevance: Do both: neutral prompts with a deterministic verify pass, and prefer externally grounded checks.

source: Moderators of correction gains across studies
finding: Moderators: verifier strength (Zhang), task type (Self-Refine math 0 vs sentiment +32), model size (Llama-2 drops 25 points, GPT-4-Turbo drops 1.5 to 3.5), and first-pass accuracy (SPOC large models).
numbers: Llama-2 GSM8K 62.0 to 36.5 vs GPT-4-Turbo 91.5 to 90.0 (Huang Table 4). Self-Refine math 0 vs sentiment GPT-4 +32.4.
limits: Compiled across studies with different setups.
agent_relevance: Weak models should skip refinement or use an external checker. Strong models with high first-pass accuracy see small gains.

source: Lee et al. (2025) ReVISE - instruction-tuned base boundary condition
finding: On an instruction-tuned Llama-3.2-1B, ordinary fine-tuning (SFT, RFT, STaR+) on GSM8K falls below the zero-shot CoT baseline. ReVISE is the only one that does not. Authors blame catastrophic forgetting and possible data contamination.
numbers: Table 3 (Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, GSM8K): all fine-tuned baselines under zero-shot CoT; ReVISE above it. Exact cells not extracted.
limits: Explanation is a hypothesis by the authors, not tested. Exact numbers not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Training a trigger on a strong chat model can erase existing skill. A scaffold with no weight change avoids this risk.
